---
title: "Linear regression"
---

Let's ask whether periodontal treatment during pregnancy
changed the baby's birth weight
in the Obstetrics and Periodontal Therapy trial
([Michalowicz et al., 2006](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa062249)).

Birth weight is a quantitative outcome,
so we use linear regression.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)
```

We'll start from `opt_clean`, made by the code below,
which keeps only live births
and labels `Group` as `control` and `treatment`.
Cleaning `opt` like this is an exercise in
[Extra practice: cleaning and tidying](07-practice-clean-and-tidy.qmd).

```{r}
opt_clean <- opt |>
  mutate(
    Birth.outcome = str_trim(Birth.outcome),
    Group = factor(Group, levels = c("C", "T"),
                   labels = c("control", "treatment"))
  ) |>
  filter(Birth.outcome == "Live birth") |>
  select(PID, Clinic, Group, Age, BMI, Birthweight, GA.at.outcome)
```

## Exercise 1: Fit a linear regression

$$
\text{birth weight} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{treatment}
$$

`treatment` is 1 for the treatment group and 0 for control.

::: {.callout-note}
## Your turn

1. Before we model, let's look at the outcome.
   Plot birth weight by group as a box plot,
   with the individual babies jittered on top.
   Do the groups look different?
2. Fit the model with `linear_reg()`,
   and show the coefficients with 95% confidence intervals.
3. What does the intercept, $\beta_0$, estimate?
4. What does the treatment coefficient, $\beta_1$, estimate?
5. Does its confidence interval include 0?
   What do you conclude?

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(opt_clean, aes(x = ____, y = ____)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3)

bw_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(____ ~ ____, data = opt_clean)

tidy(bw_fit, conf.int = ____)
```
:::

For more practice,
including a t-test, covariates, residuals, and gestational age,
see [Extra practice: linear regression](08-practice-linear-regression.qmd).
